extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (applicants, prosecutors, opponents) working before the EPO; patent attorneys and in-house counsel concerned with inventive step evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing when post‑published evidence (PPE) may be relied on to demonstrate a technical effect in support of inventive step under EPO practice as clarified by Enlarged Board Opinion G2/21. Focuses on the viewpoint of the skilled person, the role of the original application and common general knowledge, and the limits on excluding PPE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free evaluation of evidence (no summary exclusion of PPE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence submitted by a patent applicant or proprietor to prove a technical effect relied upon for acknowledgement for inventive step of the claimed subject-matter may not be disregarded solely on the ground that such evidence, on which the effect rests, had not been public before the filing date of the patent ensued and was filed after that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBoA holds that the EPO principle of free evaluation of evidence applies universally and PPE cannot be automatically excluded merely because it was generated or published after the filing date. Deciders must consider the PPE on its merits rather than summarily refusing it for being post-file date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant viewpoint: skilled person with common general knowledge and application as filed
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant view for assessing admissibility of PPE is that of the skilled person, taking into account the common general knowledge available at the filing date and the content of the application as originally filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All questions of admissibility of PPE (and of technical teaching) are to be assessed from what the notional skilled person would understand at the effective filing date, using only the original application disclosure plus the common general knowledge at that time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical teaching as the reference standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The core issue is what the skilled person, operating on the basis of common general knowledge, understands on the filing date from the application as originally filed as the technical teaching of the claimed invention (or claimed subject-matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the 'technical teaching' of the claimed invention in light of the filed application and common general knowledge — this is the baseline against which PPE is compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headnote 2 two cumulative conditions for relying on PPE
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent applicant or proprietor may rely upon a technical effect for inventive step if the skilled person, having the common general knowledge in mind, and based on the application as originally filed, would derive said effect as being encompassed by the technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both limb(s) are expressed conjunctively ('and') in Headnote 2. Deciders must therefore check (1) whether the skilled person would derive the asserted effect as encompassed by the technical teaching, and (2) whether that effect is embodied by the same originally disclosed invention. If both are affirmative, PPE may be used to support inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPE must not change the nature of the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical effect relied upon, even at a later stage, needs to be encompassed by that technical teaching and to embody the same invention, because such an effect does not change the nature of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the technical effect shown by PPE would effectively change the nature of the claimed invention (i.e., goes beyond the technical teaching/what was originally disclosed), that PPE-based effect should be excluded from assessment of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timepoint for assessment is the effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant timepoint for the skilled person's common general knowledge and for assessing what is derivable from the application remains the effective filing date of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asking what the skilled person would derive from the application as filed (and whether an asserted effect is encompassed/embodied), use only the state of the art/common general knowledge as of the filing date, not later knowledge from PPE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility is not a distinct legal requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'plausibility' found in boards' case law does not amount to a distinctive legal concept or a specific patent-law requirement under the EPC; it is a generic catchword used in jurisprudence and by users of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBoA rejected framing admissibility in terms of 'ab initio plausibility' versus 'ab initio implausibility' as formal categories; instead courts/boards should focus on the technical teaching test described above rather than applying an independent 'plausibility' legal threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical two-step assessment procedure (recommended steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an applicant may rely on PPE by: first identifying the technical teaching of the claimed invention in light of the application and common general knowledge; then considering whether the content of the PPE (the technical effect relied upon) is encompassed by that technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PPE effect is encompassed and embodied by the original technical teaching, it 'does not change the nature of the claimed invention' and may be used to support inventive step. If not, it should be excluded from the inventive-step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity/interpretation of the two limbs (need for case-by-case application)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBoA recognizes some 'abstractness' in the criteria and the conjunctive wording of Headnote 2 raises interpretive questions about how 'encompassed by the technical teaching' differs from 'embodied by the same originally disclosed invention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deciding bodies (boards, examiners, courts) will need to interpret and apply the guiding principles on a case-by-case basis; the EBoA intended flexible, principle-based guidance rather than rigid formal categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on technological advancement as guiding value
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBoA emphasizes that patenting is about advancing technology and the extent to which the skilled person recognizes such an advance in the application should be the standard by which reliance on further data is assessed when rewarding that enrichment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating PPE, consider whether the asserted technical effect reflects an advance already communicated by the application to the skilled person; PPE that merely supplies evidence of an advance already within the original teaching is more likely to be admissible.
